newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE Albania envoy warns conflict could spread.
newsitem.headline: OSCE Albania envoy warns conflict could spread.

text.p: Former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky warned on Thursday that the conflict in Albania which has claimed 20 lives could spread through the Balkans, German radio reported.
"There is a danger that the conflict in Albania could expand to other areas in the Balkans," Vranitzky, now a special envoy to Albania for the OSCE, said in an interview with Deutsche Welle radio.

He said Albanian President Sali Berisha was not opposed to his fact-finding mission on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation, but no date has yet been set for the visit. "The Albania mission from the OSCE will take place as planned," he said.
He said he assured Berisha by telephone on Thursday that the OSCE delegation would not "prosecute him like an enemy." Berisha was important for a peaceful resolution of the conflict, he said.

After violent protests, sparked by the collapse of several get-rich-quick investment schemes, erupted in Albania's south, a night-time curfew was ordered and troops were called in to quell the disturbances.

The 54-member OSCE, Europe's top security body, appointed Vranitzky on Tuesday to go to Albania to assess the situation. He said Albanian officials told the OSCE on Wednesday that the visit "was not welcome" but he still expected to travel to Tirana "in the next few days."

"Politically, the aim is that the OSCE has to take action at a very early stage to prevent a second Balkan catastrophy, after the long-sought and hard-won solution in Bosnia," Vranitzky told a news conference earlier in the day.

He said he had been instructed to seek dialogue with all political forces in the country, but declined to speculate on the outcome of his mission. "I will refrain from any premature euphoria about its success," he said.
He said Berisha had told him during a long phone conversation that the situation in Albania was "very serious" but he had no intention of stepping up military action to quash unrest in the south.
"The president said that he did not have the intention to intensify military (actions). But from here, it is of course hard to judge what is really going on in the south," Vranitzky said.
Vranitzky told Deutsche Welle radio that the OSCE troika of Swiss, Danish and Polish foreign ministers left for Albania on Thursday.

A delegation from the Council of Europe, which promotes democracy and human rights, is already in Albania and a European Union mission headed by the Dutch foreign minister is due to arrive there on Friday.

The OSCE instructed Vranitzky to assure Berisha's government of its readiness to assist in resolving the crisis that has engulfed the country, "possibly in cooperation with other relevant international organisations."
"The most important goal is to make clear to the Albanians that we come not as enemies, but as members of a group which they also belong to," Vranitzky said.
